question: What is a jurat?

options.text: The notary's certificate that a document was sworn to (or affirmed) and signed in the notary's presence
options.why: Correct. A jurat certifies two facts: an oath or affirmation was taken, and the signature was made in front of the notary.

options.text: The notary's certificate that a signer acknowledged an earlier signature
options.why: Wrong. That is an acknowledgment certificate.

options.text: A certified copy of a sworn statement
options.why: Wrong. A jurat is a certificate about the signing, not a copy.

options.text: A notary's record book entry
options.why: Wrong. The record entry is separate from the certificate on the document.

explanation: A jurat certifies that the signer took an oath or affirmation and signed in front of the notary.

question: Which typical wording appears in a jurat?

options.text: "Sworn to and subscribed before me on (date)."
options.why: Correct. 'Sworn to' shows the oath and 'subscribed' means signed, both before the notary.

options.text: "This instrument was acknowledged before me on (date)."
options.why: Wrong. That is acknowledgment wording.

options.text: "I certify this is a true copy."
options.why: Wrong. That is copy-certification language.

options.text: "Witnessed but not sworn on (date)."
options.why: Wrong. A jurat requires an oath, so 'not sworn' contradicts it.

explanation: "Sworn to and subscribed before me" is the standard jurat language. "Subscribed" means signed.

question: For a jurat, the signer must:

options.text: Sign in the notary's presence and swear or affirm to the contents
options.why: Correct. Both elements are required for a jurat.

options.text: Sign at any time before the appointment
options.why: Wrong. Signing in advance is allowed for acknowledgments, not jurats.

options.text: Have the document reviewed by the notary for accuracy
options.why: Wrong. The notary doesn't check the accuracy of the statements.

options.text: Bring two witnesses
options.why: Wrong. Jurats don't require witnesses.

explanation: A jurat requires both an oath or affirmation and signing in the notary's presence.

question: What is the difference between an oath and an affirmation?

options.text: An oath is a pledge to a Supreme Being; an affirmation is a solemn pledge on personal honor. Both carry the same legal weight.
options.why: Correct. The only difference is the religious reference; a false statement under either can be perjury.

options.text: An affirmation is not legally binding
options.why: Wrong. An affirmation is fully binding and carries perjury penalties.

options.text: An oath is used only in court
options.why: Wrong. Notaries administer oaths for affidavits and other documents outside court.

options.text: An affirmation requires a witness; an oath does not
options.why: Wrong. Neither requires an extra witness.

explanation: An affirmation is the legal equivalent of an oath for people who prefer not to swear to a deity. Either way, false statements can be perjury.

question: Who decides whether a signer takes an oath or an affirmation?

options.text: The signer
options.why: Correct. It's a matter of the signer's conscience, so the signer chooses.

options.text: The notary
options.why: Wrong. A notary can't force a religious oath on someone who prefers to affirm.

options.text: The document's preparer
options.why: Wrong. The preparer doesn't control how the signer is sworn.

options.text: Whichever the certificate wording says, regardless of the signer's wishes
options.why: Wrong. If the signer affirms, the wording can say 'sworn to (or affirmed)'; the signer's choice governs.

explanation: The person being sworn chooses. The notary should offer an affirmation to anyone who prefers it.

question: What is an affidavit?

options.text: A written statement sworn to or affirmed before an officer authorized to administer oaths
options.why: Correct. This matches the definition in Gov't Code §312.011.

options.text: Any document with a notary seal
options.why: Wrong. A deed with an acknowledgment carries a seal but isn't an affidavit.

options.text: A contract between two parties
options.why: Wrong. A contract is an agreement; an affidavit is a sworn statement of facts.

options.text: A copy of a court order
options.why: Wrong. A court order is issued by a judge, not sworn by a party.

explanation: An affidavit is a written statement of facts confirmed by oath or affirmation, and is typically completed with a jurat.

question: Which is the key difference between a jurat and an acknowledgment?

options.text: A jurat requires an oath or affirmation and signing in the notary's presence; an acknowledgment does not
options.why: Correct. These two features set the jurat apart.

options.text: An acknowledgment requires an oath; a jurat does not
options.why: Wrong. This reverses the rule.

options.text: A jurat may be done by phone
options.why: Wrong. Neither act may be done by phone; remote acts require a commissioned online notary using audio-video.

options.text: There is no difference
options.why: Wrong. The two acts certify different things and aren't interchangeable.

explanation: In a jurat the signer swears to the contents and signs in front of the notary. In an acknowledgment the signer acknowledges a signature already made, without an oath.
source: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §121.004; Texas SOS notary guidance

question: When completing a jurat, is the notary responsible for verifying that the affidavit's statements are true?

options.text: No; the signer is responsible for the truth of what they swear to
options.why: Correct. The notary administers the oath; the signer answers for the truth, under penalty of perjury.

options.text: Yes; the notary must check every fact
options.why: Wrong. Notaries have neither the duty nor the means to verify facts.

options.text: Only for financial documents
options.why: Wrong. No category of document makes the notary a fact-checker.

options.text: Only if the notary knows the signer
options.why: Wrong. Knowing the signer affects identification, not responsibility for the contents.

explanation: The notary administers the oath and identifies the signer. Truthfulness is the signer's responsibility, under penalty of perjury.

question: A person knowingly makes a false statement in a sworn affidavit. Who may be guilty of perjury?

options.text: The person who made the false statement
options.why: Correct. Under Penal Code §37.02, perjury is committed by the person who makes a false statement under oath.

options.text: The notary who administered the oath
options.why: Wrong. The notary isn't the one making the statement, unless they knowingly took part in the fraud.

options.text: The notary's surety company
options.why: Wrong. A surety can be liable for damages under the bond but can't commit perjury.

options.text: No one, because affidavits are not court documents
options.why: Wrong. Perjury covers false sworn statements outside court too.

explanation: Perjury is committed by the person who makes a false statement under oath, not by the officer administering it.

question: How should a notary properly administer an oath for a jurat?

options.text: Have the signer raise their right hand (if willing) and respond aloud to a spoken oath, such as "Do you solemnly swear that the statements in this document are true?"
options.why: Correct. The oath is spoken by the notary and answered aloud by the signer; raising a hand is customary but optional.

options.text: Hand over the document and assume signing is enough
options.why: Wrong. Signing alone isn't an oath; skipping the oath makes the jurat false.

options.text: Ask the signer to initial a box saying they were sworn
options.why: Wrong. Initials can't replace an oath actually given.

options.text: Send the oath wording by text message
options.why: Wrong. A traditional oath is given in person, aloud.

explanation: An oath must actually be given: the notary speaks it and the signer answers affirmatively. Signing alone is not an oath.

question: A signer arrives with an affidavit already signed and wants a jurat. The notary should:

options.text: Administer the oath and have the signer sign again (for example, a fresh unsigned copy) in the notary's presence
options.why: Correct. A jurat certifies signing in front of the notary, so a new signature must be made after the oath.

options.text: Complete the jurat as is
options.why: Wrong. The certificate would falsely say the document was signed before the notary.

options.text: Convert it to an acknowledgment without asking
options.why: Wrong. Changing the type of act is the signer's (or recipient's) decision, not the notary's.

options.text: Refuse; affidavits cannot be notarized once signed
options.why: Wrong. Re-signing in the notary's presence solves the problem.

explanation: A jurat certifies signing in the notary's presence, so the signature must be made after the oath, in front of the notary.

question: Under Texas law, which officers may administer oaths?

options.text: Notaries public are among the officers authorized to administer oaths
options.why: Correct. Gov't Code §602.002 lists notaries along with judges, clerks and other officers.

options.text: Only judges
options.why: Wrong. The statute names many officers, including notaries.

options.text: Only county clerks
options.why: Wrong. Clerks can, but so can notaries and others.

options.text: Only attorneys
options.why: Wrong. Being an attorney doesn't confer oath-giving power; the statute lists officers by office.

explanation: Texas law lists notaries public among the officers who may administer oaths.

question: May a traditional Texas notary administer an oath over the phone to a signer in another city?

options.text: No; for a traditional notarization the signer must appear in the notary's physical presence
options.why: Correct. Traditional acts require physical presence; remote acts are allowed only for online notaries using audio-video.

options.text: Yes, if the notary recognizes the signer's voice
options.why: Wrong. Voice recognition isn't personal appearance.

options.text: Yes, if the signer faxes the signed page
options.why: Wrong. A fax shows neither appearance nor signing in the notary's presence.

options.text: Yes, for affidavits only
options.why: Wrong. Affidavits need in-person appearance like any other traditional act.

explanation: Traditional acts require personal appearance. Remote acts are allowed only through a commissioned online notary using audio-video technology.

question: A signer refuses to take either an oath or an affirmation but wants a jurat. The notary should:

options.text: Decline to complete the jurat
options.why: Correct. A jurat certifies an oath or affirmation; with neither, the certificate would be false.

options.text: Complete it, since the signer signed in person
options.why: Wrong. Signing in person is only half of a jurat.

options.text: Complete it and write 'not sworn' beside the seal
options.why: Wrong. That contradicts the certificate rather than fixing it.

options.text: Complete it if the signer pays double
options.why: Wrong. Payment doesn't change the facts, and overcharging breaks the fee rules.

explanation: A jurat certifies that an oath or affirmation was taken. Without one, the certificate would be false.

question: Must a Texas notary identify the signer before completing a jurat?

options.text: Yes; the signer's identity must be established and recorded as for any notarial act
options.why: Correct. The §406.014 record requires the identification method for each act, jurats included.

options.text: No; an oath is enough
options.why: Wrong. An oath from an unidentified person doesn't establish who swore.

options.text: Only if the affidavit is longer than one page
options.why: Wrong. Document length has no bearing on identification.

options.text: Only for out-of-state signers
options.why: Wrong. Every signer must be identified, wherever they live.

explanation: The notary record must show how each signer was identified, so identification is required for jurats as well as acknowledgments.

question: Which statement is a proper affirmation?

options.text: "Do you solemnly affirm, under penalty of perjury, that the statements in this document are true?"
options.why: Correct. It's solemn, carries perjury consequences and makes no reference to a deity.

options.text: "Do you promise to try your best to be accurate?"
options.why: Wrong. A promise to 'try' isn't a solemn declaration of truth.

options.text: "Is this your signature?"
options.why: Wrong. This is closer to an acknowledgment question and says nothing about truth.

options.text: "Did someone else prepare this document for you?"
options.why: Wrong. Who prepared the document doesn't matter to an affirmation.

explanation: An affirmation is a solemn declaration made under penalty of perjury, without reference to a Supreme Being.
